newsitem.title: UK: British election to curb sterling Eurobond supply.
newsitem.headline: British election to curb sterling Eurobond supply.

text.p: Primary market supply of sterling Eurobonds will be curbed in the run-up to the May 1 British election after a robust start to the year for the sector, bankers said on Monday.
"It will be a choppy period in the run-up to the election and market conditions will not be optimum," a syndicate manager at a British bank said.
A syndicate official at a U.S. investment bank said the sterling Eurobond market was currently "soggy" and needed time to consolidate after the pound's recent slip.
"International investors will prefer to wait on the sidelines until after the election," he said.
British Prime Minister John Major announced on Monday after seeking the dissolution of Parliament from Queen Elizabeth that an election would take place on Thursday, May 1.

Retail-targeted deals in particular would be inhibited by uncertainty before the election, while institutionally-aimed transactions might be more resilient to the long election campaign period, dealers said.
A collateralised Housing Association deal worth nearly 1.0 billion stg and targeted at institutional investors is expected to be launched this week by NatWest Capital Markets.
But dealers away from the lead said it would be difficult to launch this asset-backed bond.
"They'll find it tough," a dealer said.

Other factors that will put a lid on new sterling supply are the pound's back-tracking from recent long-term highs against the mark, the upcoming Easter holiday and a 10-year gilt auction, traders said.
At 1300 GMT the pound was at 2.6885 marks. On March 6, it hit a high around 2.7730 marks, its best level since the pound's exit from the European exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.
The sterling Eurobond sector has flourished this year on the back of the robust pound and the relatively high yields available in Britain.
Sterling is perceived as a "safe haven" currency, unlikely to join the European economic and monetary union single currency at the outset.
In terms of the secondary market, dealers said activity was already nervous following U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's recent comments about credit markets.

"The market has been very nervous in the past week -- spreads have widened in the past week by roughly five basis points across the board on anything you choose to look at -- so I don't think the announcement of an election will make much difference now (to sterling Eurobond spreads)," an analyst at a British bank said.

A jumbo sterling bond from U.S. home loan agency Fannie Mae -- a 1.25 billion stg global offering due June 2002 -- was trading at a yield spread of 14/12 basis points at midday, versus a launch spread of eight b.p.
-- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7718
That eight b.p. launch spread was on a 250 million stg increase of the Fannie Mae deal made on March 5, when sterling was close to its peak.
The original 1.0 billion stg offering was issued February 11 at a 10 b.p. spread.
Joint lead manager BZW said the deal was now at 12/11 b.p.
While the Fannie Mae deal was the biggest sterling bond for some time, a host of FTSE-100 companies have tapped the market so far this year with smaller deals.

They include BAA with a 200 million stg 10-year funding, J. Sainsbury with a 200 million stg June 2002 issue and Land Securities with a 210 million stg convertible bond. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7718
